In recent weeks, a claim has circulated widely on social media platforms, asserting that inhaling steam daily for a week can eliminate the coronavirus from the body. This assertion has garnered considerable attention, with users sharing anecdotes and purported remedies involving steam inhalation as a preventative or curative measure against COVID-19. Given the seriousness of the ongoing pandemic and the importance of accurate health information, it is crucial to examine the validity of this claim.

The core of the claim is that the act of inhaling steam—usually by leaning over a bowl of hot water and covering the head with a towel—can kill or eliminate the coronavirus, thereby preventing or curing COVID-19. Proponents often suggest adding substances such as eucalyptus oil, menthol, or other herbal ingredients to the water, believing these augment the supposed antiviral effects.

To assess this claim, it is important to understand how the coronavirus infects the body. The virus primarily enters through the nose and mouth, attaching itself to cells in the respiratory tract. Once inside, it multiplies and can cause a range of symptoms, from mild colds to severe respiratory distress. The notion behind steam inhalation as a cure likely stems from its long-standing use as a home remedy for congestion and sinus relief. Steam can temporarily soothe irritated airways and loosen mucus, making breathing easier for those suffering from colds, allergies, or other respiratory conditions.

However, there is no scientific evidence to support the idea that steam inhalation can kill the coronavirus or eliminate it from the respiratory system. The virus resides deep within the body's cells, and steam does not reach the lower respiratory tract where the virus often causes the most harm. Additionally, the temperatures required to inactivate the virus are far higher than those that are safe for human inhalation. Attempting to inhale steam at excessively high temperatures can result in burns or other injuries, and experts warn against using this method as a treatment for COVID-19.

Major health organizations and medical professionals have repeatedly emphasized that steam inhalation should not be considered a cure or preventive measure for COVID-19. While it may offer symptomatic relief for some upper respiratory discomforts, it does not eliminate the virus or prevent infection. The most effective strategies for preventing COVID-19 remain vaccination, proper hand hygiene, mask-wearing in crowded or high-risk settings, and maintaining physical distance from others.

In conclusion, the claim that inhaling steam for a week can eliminate the coronavirus is false. Steam inhalation may provide temporary comfort for some respiratory symptoms, but it does not kill the virus or cure COVID-19. Relying on unproven remedies can offer a false sense of security and may delay individuals from seeking appropriate medical care. For protection against COVID-19, it is essential to follow evidence-based guidelines provided by public health authorities.

Par mohou dočasně uklidnit zánětlivé dýchací cesty a uvolnit sliznici, čímž zlepší dýchání u lidí trpících chřipkou, alergií nebo jinými dýchacími potížemi.

I když může nabízet dočasnou úlevu při některých horních dýchacích potížích, neodstraňuje viru ani nezabrání infekci. Nejúčinnější strategie pro prevenci nemoci COVID-19 zůstávají vakcinace, správná hygiena rukou, použití roušek ve zplodinách nebo v rizikových situacích a udržování fyzické vzdálenosti od ostatních lidí.

Závěrem je, že tvrzení, že vdechnutí par po týden může odstranit koronaviru, je nepravdivé. K ochraně proti nemoci COVID-19 je důležité dodržovat důkazové doporučení poskytovaná veřejnými zdravotními orgány.

A claim that the Pirbright Institute, allegedly funded by Bill Gates, patented the coronavirus prior to the COVID-19 outbreak has again made the rounds on social media. This assertion implies a connection between the institute, Bill Gates, and the origins of the novel coronavirus responsible for the global pandemic. To assess this claim, it is essential to examine the patent in question, the role of the Pirbright Institute, and the extent of Bill Gates’ involvement.

The Pirbright Institute, based in the United Kingdom, is a well-known research center focusing primarily on viruses that affect animals, particularly livestock. In 2015, the institute was granted a patent related to a form of coronavirus. However, the specifics of this patent are often misunderstood or misrepresented in online discussions.

The patent, awarded in 2015, covers a weakened form of a coronavirus that is specific to avian species, particularly chickens. This research was part of longstanding efforts to develop vaccines to prevent certain diseases in poultry, such as infectious bronchitis virus—a type of coronavirus that affects chickens but not humans. The patent does not cover the novel coronavirus, known as SARS-CoV-2, which emerged in 2019 and caused the COVID-19 pandemic. There is no evidence that the patented virus or technology is related to the human coronavirus responsible for the global outbreak.

The confusion appears to stem from the broad use of the term “coronavirus.” Coronaviruses are a large family of viruses, some of which cause illnesses in animals and others in humans, ranging from the common cold to more severe diseases like SARS, MERS, and COVID-19. The Pirbright Institute’s work was confined to animal health and did not involve research on human-infecting coronaviruses.

Regarding funding, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation has provided grants to many scientific institutions worldwide, including the Pirbright Institute. These grants supported research into animal diseases and vaccine development but were not directed toward creating or patenting viruses for humans. The financial support from the Gates Foundation to Pirbright is a matter of public record and pertains to animal health research, not to the development or patenting of the novel coronavirus.

There is no credible evidence to support the claim that the Pirbright Institute, with funding from Bill Gates, patented the coronavirus responsible for COVID-19 before the outbreak. The patent in question is unrelated to SARS-CoV-2 and addresses only animal diseases. This persistent misinformation appears to conflate unrelated facts to suggest a connection that does not exist.

In summary, the claim that Bill Gates-funded Pirbright Institute patented the coronavirus before the outbreak is misleading. The patented virus is specific to poultry, not humans, and the Gates Foundation’s involvement is limited to supporting animal health research. The origins of the novel coronavirus are unrelated to the Pirbright Institute’s patent or its research activities.

article_content:
As Covid-19 vaccines became available to the public, millions of people turned to their phones and computers to register for vaccination appointments. In this context, a social media post has warned: “Covid vaccine registration on phone lands people in phishing net.” This claim raises concerns that individuals attempting to register for the Covid vaccine via their smartphones may fall victim to phishing schemes. To assess the validity of this warning, it is essential to examine the context of vaccine registration processes, the prevalence of phishing attempts related to Covid-19, and the steps necessary for safe registration.

When Covid-19 vaccination drives were first launched, health authorities and governments set up official websites and apps to facilitate mass registration. These platforms required individuals to provide personal information such as names, dates of birth, and contact details. As registration demand surged, cybercriminals saw an opportunity to exploit public urgency and confusion. Reports from the early stages of the vaccine rollout noted an uptick in phishing attempts, including fake registration websites and fraudulent messages inviting users to schedule vaccine appointments. These schemes often mimicked the appearance of legitimate government or health service websites, tricking users into sharing sensitive data.

Phishing is a form of cybercrime in which attackers impersonate trustworthy entities to steal information, such as passwords or financial data. During the pandemic, phishing campaigns frequently included messages about Covid-19 vaccines, testing, and relief payments. Some attacks involved text messages, emails, or even phone calls that directed recipients to malicious links, requesting personal or payment information under the guise of vaccine registration.

However, it is critical to clarify that registering for the Covid vaccine on a phone, in itself, does not automatically expose someone to phishing. The risk arises when individuals use unofficial or suspicious links, respond to unsolicited messages, or enter personal information on fraudulent websites. Official vaccine registration portals operated by governments and recognized health organizations implemented security measures to protect users. Instructing the public to access these resources directly—rather than through links in messages or social media—was a key part of public awareness campaigns.

Fact-checking the core claim, the warning in the social media post is rooted in a genuine risk: phishing scams did target individuals seeking to register for the Covid vaccine, especially via mobile devices. Nonetheless, the wording may be misleading by implying that all phone-based vaccine registration is unsafe. The actual threat comes from engaging with unofficial or fraudulent sources, not from the act of registering by phone itself.

In conclusion, while phishing scams did exploit the Covid vaccine registration process, especially among mobile users, individuals following official channels faced minimal risk. The claim highlights a real cybersecurity concern but overstates the inevitability of falling into a phishing scheme simply by registering for a vaccine on a phone. As always, users should remain vigilant, verify website authenticity, and avoid clicking on suspicious links to ensure their safety during online processes.

A recent social media post claims that a New York Times (NYT) ranking shows the top four Covid-19 vaccines are Chinese-made. This assertion has attracted significant attention online, raising questions about the accuracy of the claim and the context in which it may have originated.

To evaluate this statement, it is important to understand how Covid-19 vaccines have been ranked or presented by major publications such as The New York Times. Since the global rollout of Covid-19 vaccines began in late 2020, various vaccines have been developed and distributed worldwide. The most widely discussed vaccines include those developed by Pfizer-BioNTech, Moderna, AstraZeneca-Oxford, Johnson & Johnson (Janssen), as well as Chinese-made vaccines like Sinopharm, Sinovac, and CanSino.

The phrase "NYT ranking" is vague. The New York Times has published numerous articles and interactive resources tracking Covid-19 vaccines, including maps and timelines showing global vaccine use, approval status, and production numbers. However, the NYT has not published a formal "ranking" that lists vaccines by effectiveness, safety, or importance. Instead, their coverage has focused on reporting regulatory approvals, distribution statistics, and efficacy data as released by health authorities and peer-reviewed studies.

Chinese-made vaccines, particularly Sinopharm and Sinovac, have played a significant role in the global vaccination effort, especially among low- and middle-income countries. Due to production scale and international agreements, these vaccines have been widely distributed across Asia, Africa, and Latin America. This widespread use has sometimes led to Chinese vaccines being among the most administered globally, particularly in terms of total doses. This might be the source of the confusion or misinterpretation in the social media claim.

However, when it comes to vaccine efficacy as reported in clinical trials and real-world studies, Western-developed vaccines such as Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna have generally shown higher efficacy rates against symptomatic Covid-19, especially against severe disease and hospitalization. Regulatory agencies in the United States, European Union, and several other regions have prioritized these vaccines in their national rollouts. The NYT’s reporting has reflected these realities, often highlighting the differences in efficacy and global distribution challenges.

There is no publicly available evidence that The New York Times has published a ranking placing Chinese-made vaccines in the top four spots by any consistent or recognized metric such as efficacy, safety, or global influence. The closest context in which Chinese vaccines might appear among "top" vaccines is in lists or charts of total doses administered globally, where Sinopharm and Sinovac have at times been among the most distributed due to large-scale use in populous countries.

In summary, the claim that a NYT ranking shows the top four Covid-19 vaccines are Chinese-made is misleading. While Chinese vaccines have been widely administered and have played an important role in the global response, The New York Times has not formally ranked them as the top four vaccines. The claim likely conflates high distribution numbers with a formal ranking or endorsement, which does not accurately reflect the nature of NYT coverage or the broader scientific consensus.

Regulaj aŭtoritatoj en Usono, Eŭropo kaj pluraj aliaj regionoj prioritizis tiujn vakcinojn en siaj naciaj distribuadoj. La raportado de Nova Yorka Tempo reflektis tiujn realojn, ofte subliniante la diferencon en efikeco kaj globaj distribuaj problemoj.

Neniu publike disponebla informo montras, ke Nova Yorka Tempo publikigis rango, kiu situas ĉinajn vakcinojn en la unuaj kvar pozicioj per iu konstanta aŭ konata metriko kiel efikeco, sekureco aŭ globa influo. La plej proksima konteksto, en kiu ĉinaj vakcinoj eble aperas inter "top" vakcinoj, estas en listoj aŭ diagramoj de totalaj dozoj administritaj globale, kie Sinopharm kaj Sinovac iam estis inter la plej distribuigitaj pro ilia ampleksa uzado en populacaj landoj.

En konkludo, la deklaro, ke NYT rango montras, ke la unuaj kvar koronavirusa vakcinoj estas ĉinaj, estas malvera. Tiamanku, ĉinaj vakcinoj havis ampleksan uzon kaj havis gravan rolon en la globa respondo, sed Nova Yorka Tempo ne oficiale rangigis ilin kiel la unuaj kvar vakcinoj. La deklaro eble konfuzis altajn distribuajn nombron kun forman rangon aŭ subskribo, kio ne precize reflektas la naturon de la NYT kovro aŭ la pli vastan sciencan konsenson.
article_summary: A social media claim alleging a New York Times ranking places Chinese-made vaccines among the top four Covid-19 vaccines is misleading. The NYT has not published a formal ranking of vaccines by efficacy or safety, though it has reported on global distribution and approval data. Chinese vaccines like Sinopharm and Sinovac are widely administered, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, but this does not equate to a formal ranking by the NYT or scientific consensus.
